concept.name: Blue-Green Deployment

relationships.description: Connects Blue-Green Deployment to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Blue-green deployment maintains two identical production environments—one active (Blue) and one idle or staging (Green)—and shifts 100% of live traffic at the load balancer or DNS layer once Green passes smoke tests, enabling sub-second rollback by reversing the router pointer.
spark.keyTakeaway: Instant rollback works only if your database schema and shared state remain backward-compatible with both versions during the cutover window.

concept.whyItMatters: In-place rolling updates mix old and new application versions simultaneously and force slow, error-prone reverse deployments when a bad build slips past CI. Blue-green isolates validation on an unexposed production clone before a single user hits it, turning cutover and rollback into deterministic, atomic routing flips.
whenToUse: Stateless HTTP/gRPC services behind an L7 load balancer (AWS ALB, Envoy, NGINX) where atomic cutover and sub-30-second rollback justify temporary 2x compute.
Compliance-heavy releases (fintech, healthcare) requiring full smoke, synthetic, and security verification on production-identical infrastructure prior to live traffic exposure.
Major runtime or OS upgrades (e.g., JVM 17 to 21, Kubernetes node pool migration) where mixing old and new pods in the same ReplicaSet risks subtle runtime incompatibilities.
whenNotToUse: Stateful monoliths or tightly coupled services that share local disk state, in-memory sessions, or non-backward-compatible database schemas without an expand-contract migration pipeline.
Cost-constrained workloads with massive GPU or high-memory footprints (e.g., 500+ H100 nodes) where doubling capacity even for 30 minutes is financially or quota-prohibitive.
High-risk algorithmic or UX changes where you need gradual 1%–10% blast-radius exposure and statistical A/B comparison—use canary deployments instead.
keyPoints: Traffic switches atomically at an L7 proxy (ALB target group swap, Kubernetes Service selector flip, or Istio VirtualService) rather than relying on DNS TTLs, which clients and ISPs routinely cache past 60s.
Database changes must follow the expand-and-contract pattern: Green runs against an additive schema (nullable columns, new tables) that Blue can still read and write safely during rollback.

Connection draining (`deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds = 30` in AWS ALB or `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` in Kubernetes) prevents mid-flight HTTP 502s when Blue instances stop accepting new requests.
Warm-up requests against Green (JIT compilation, connection pool priming, local cache hydration) must complete before cutover to avoid a cold-start latency spike at 100% traffic.
Keep Blue running in warm standby for a defined bake window (typically 15–60 minutes) after cutover so rollback is a router flip rather than a fresh provision.

examples.title: AWS ECS + ALB Target Group Swap for a Checkout API
examples.scenario: A payments service running 24 ECS Fargate tasks behind an AWS Application Load Balancer deploys v4.12 to the Green target group on port 8080, runs 120 synthetic checkout assertions against a private test listener on port 8443, and warms HikariCP pools.
examples.outcome: CodeDeploy shifts listener rule priority from Blue to Green in <2 seconds with a 30-second connection drain on Blue. When a memory leak surfaces 12 minutes later, operators revert the ALB listener rule to Blue in 1.5 seconds with zero dropped transactions.

examples.title: Kubernetes Service Selector Cutover with Expand-Contract PostgreSQL Migration
examples.scenario: An order-fulfillment service needs to rename `shipping_tier` to `fulfillment_class`. A pre-deploy Flyway job adds `fulfillment_class` as nullable, installs a dual-write trigger, and backfills 40M rows in 10k-row batches before Green pods deploy.
examples.outcome: Flipping `kubectl patch svc orders -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"slot":"green"}}}'` cuts traffic cleanly. Both Blue and Green remain schema-compatible for 24 hours, after which a contract migration drops the legacy trigger and `shipping_tier` column.

tradeOffs.pro: Ephemeral Green provisioning via Terraform/ECS/K8s incurs 2x compute only during the 20–60 minute deploy and bake window.
tradeOffs.con: Maintaining a permanent warm standby doubles baseline compute costs and can hit cloud vCPU or IP-subnet exhaustion limits.

tradeOffs.pro: Cutover and rollback are O(1) routing operations completing in seconds, unaffected by artifact build or container pull times.
tradeOffs.con: Because 100% of traffic shifts at once, a latent bug under full production concurrency hits all users simultaneously until rollback triggers.

tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates version-skew bugs between Blue and Green application instances because only one version serves live users at a time.
tradeOffs.con: Shifts complexity to external state: DB schemas, Kafka consumer offsets, and Redis serialization formats must stay dual-compatible.

failureModes.name: Destructive Schema Migration Breaks Rollback
failureModes.description: Green drops a column or alters a data type in-place before cutover; when Green fails and traffic reverts to Blue, Blue crashes with SQL errors.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce expand-and-contract migrations in CI: block `DROP COLUMN`, `RENAME`, or `NOT NULL` without defaults until at least one release cycle after Green is permanent.

failureModes.name: Stale DNS Caching Extends Split-Brain Traffic
failureModes.description: Switching via Route 53 DNS even with TTL=60s leaves JVM and corporate resolvers caching Blue's IP for 5–15 minutes, splitting writes across versions.
failureModes.mitigation: Perform cutover at an L7 reverse proxy or load balancer (ALB, Envoy, Cloudflare Workers) with a fixed Anycast/VIP endpoint.

failureModes.name: Cold-Start Latency & Cache Stampede on Green
failureModes.description: Green passes low-RPS health checks but suffers p99 spikes from 40ms to 1,800ms at 100% traffic due to empty JVM JIT tiers and cold Redis/local caches.
failureModes.mitigation: Replay shadow traffic or run a pre-cutover warm-up script hitting top 1,000 hot keys before flipping the production listener.

failureModes.name: Long-Lived WebSockets or gRPC Streams Dropped
failureModes.description: Aggressive target deregistration terminates active WebSocket or HTTP/2 streams immediately on cutover, triggering client reconnect storms.
failureModes.mitigation: Configure `GOAWAY` frames on HTTP/2/gRPC and 60–300s `deregistration_delay` with jittered client reconnect backoff.

commonMistakes: Using DNS swaps instead of L7 load balancer target switching, causing unpredictable client-side caching delays.
Running `DROP` or destructive `ALTER` migrations in the same deployment step as the Green rollout.
Terminating the Blue environment immediately after cutover instead of keeping it warm through the bake window.
Sharing a single non-namespaced Redis key prefix between Blue and Green when serialized DTO formats change.
Assuming `/health` returning HTTP 200 means Green is warmed up for full production concurrency.

sections.content:
## The idea

Blue-green deployment decouples **deployment** (provisioning new compute, pulling containers, running migrations, verifying health) from **release** (exposing live user traffic). Two parallel environments—Blue (currently live) and Green (newly provisioned)—sit behind a single routing control plane. Until Green passes automated smoke and synthetic checks on an isolated test port or internal header, zero external users touch it. Release is an atomic pointer swap at the router, and rollback is the exact inverse pointer swap.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an orders API handling 4,000 RPS behind an AWS Application Load Balancer:

1. **Baseline**: ALB listener `:443` forwards 100% of traffic to `tg-orders-blue` (32 ECS tasks, v2.14.0). `tg-orders-green` has 0 tasks.
2. **Provision & Expand**: CI runs an additive Flyway migration (`ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN tax_jurisdiction VARCHAR(16) NULL`) and provisions 32 tasks of v2.15.0 in `tg-orders-green`.
3. **Isolated Verification**: An internal ALB listener on `:8443` routes synthetic smoke tests and a 5-minute warm-up load (priming JVM C2 JIT and HikariCP's 20-connection pools per task) exclusively to `tg-orders-green`.
4. **Atomic Cutover**: The ALB listener rule on `:443` switches its forward target from `tg-orders-blue` to `tg-orders-green`. New TCP/TLS connections and HTTP requests immediately land on Green.
5. **Drain & Bake**: `tg-orders-blue` enters a 30-second deregistration delay to finish in-flight requests, then remains idle for a 30-minute bake window. If p99 latency or 5xx rate breaches SLOs, the listener flips back to `tg-orders-blue` in <2 seconds. Otherwise, Blue tasks are scaled to 0.

sections.content:
## Cutover mechanisms compared

The choice of routing layer dictates cutover atomicity, rollback latency, and blast radius during transition. L7 reverse proxies (ALB, Envoy, NGINX) and Kubernetes Services update endpoint tables inside your VPC in milliseconds. DNS-based switching (Route 53 weighted records) is the weakest mechanism for zero-downtime swaps because recursive resolvers, JVM `networkaddress.cache.ttl`, and mobile carriers ignore low TTLs, leaving 5–20% of traffic hitting Blue long after cutover.

## Deployment strategies side by side

| Dimension | Blue-Green | Rolling Update | Canary Deployment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Peak Compute Overhead** | 200% (2x during cutover/bake) | 105%–125% (`maxSurge`) | 105%–120% |
| **Cutover Granularity** | 0% -> 100% atomic | Pod-by-pod / batch | 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% |
| **Rollback Latency** | <5 seconds (router flip) | Minutes (re-pull/re-schedule) | <10 seconds (weight to 0%) |
| **Version Skew in Prod** | None (single active slot) | High (old + new coexist) | Controlled (subset of traffic) |
| **DB Schema Requirement** | Expand-contract for rollback | Expand-contract mandatory | Expand-contract mandatory |

## Failure modes

1. **Backward-Incompatible State**: Dropping a column, changing a Kafka Avro schema without `BACKWARD` compatibility, or altering a Redis JSON key structure breaks Blue on rollback. Always separate `expand` (pre-deploy) from `contract` (post-bake).
2. **Connection Pool Exhaustion**: During the 30-minute bake window, both Blue (idle pools) and Green (active pools) hold open connections to PostgreSQL. If `max_connections` is 500 and each slot opens 320 connections, Green fails to boot. Use PgBouncer/RDS Proxy in transaction pooling mode.
3. **Async Queue / Cron Duplication**: Background workers (SQS consumers, Kafka groups, Kubernetes CronJobs) are not gated by the HTTP load balancer. Pause or fence Blue's background consumers before starting Green's, or ensure strict idempotency keys.

## Handling async consumers and WebSockets

Blue-green works cleanly for request-response HTTP/gRPC, but async workers and stateful connections need explicit coordination. For Kafka consumers, deploying Green into the same consumer group triggers a rebalance storm; instead, use a feature flag or leader-election lease in ZooKeeper/etcd so only the active color polls partitions. For WebSockets or gRPC streaming, set `deregistration_delay` to match your longest expected session or emit HTTP/2 `GOAWAY` frames from Blue so clients reconnect with exponential jitter onto Green.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Verify L7 cutover mechanism (ALB target group, Envoy cluster weight, or K8s Service selector) without relying on DNS TTLs.
- [ ] Enforce expand-and-contract database migrations via CI linting (block destructive DDL on live tables).
- [ ] Size database connection pools (or deploy PgBouncer) to accommodate 2x application instances during overlap.
- [ ] Configure graceful shutdown (`SIGTERM` -> fail `/readyz` -> wait `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` >= `deregistration_delay`).
- [ ] Warm up Green caches, JIT, and connection pools via isolated `:8443` or shadow traffic before flipping `:443`.
- [ ] Keep Blue warm for at least 15–30 minutes post-cutover and automate rollback on 5xx or p99 SLO burn.

interviewProblems.title: Blue-Green Deployment
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Blue-Green Deployment. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Blue-green deployment maintains two identical production environments—one active (Blue) and one idle or staging (Green)—and shifts 100% of live traffic at the load balancer or DNS layer once Green passes smoke tests, enabling sub-second rollback by reversing the router pointer.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Green Environment applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Shared PostgreSQL.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Shared PostgreSQL experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Enforce expand-and-contract migrations in CI: block `DROP COLUMN`, `RENAME`, or `NOT NULL` without defaults until at least one release cycle after Green is permanent.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Instant rollback works only if your database schema and shared state remain backward-compatible with both versions during the cutover window.
Avoid trap: Using DNS swaps instead of L7 load balancer target switching, causing unpredictable client-side caching delays.
Avoid trap: Running `DROP` or destructive `ALTER` migrations in the same deployment step as the Green rollout.
When to reach for it: Stateless HTTP/gRPC services behind an L7 load balancer (AWS ALB, Envoy, NGINX) where atomic cutover and sub-30-second rollback justify temporary 2x compute.
When to reach for it: Compliance-heavy releases (fintech, healthcare) requiring full smoke, synthetic, and security verification on production-identical infrastructure prior to live traffic exposure.

putItTogether.title: Putting Blue Green Deployment Together
putItTogether.summary: Instant rollback works only if your database schema and shared state remain backward-compatible with both versions during the cutover window.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Blue Green Deployment before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: CodeDeploy shifts listener rule priority from Blue to Green in <2 seconds with a 30-second connection drain on Blue. When a memory leak surfaces 12 minutes later, operators revert the ALB listener rule to Blue in 1.5 seconds with zero dropped transactions.
